# The Flood Point


[Chelsey Sassine](https://medium.com/@chelseysassine?source=post_page---byline--b2abfd2fdcd9------------------------------------------)


4 min read


·


2 hours ago

*Why you can’t ship faster than you can see*


Press enter or click to view image in full size


In college, one of my chemical engineering labs had us run a distillation column made of glass. Distillation separates a mixture by boiling it. A heater at the bottom boils the mixture, and the vapor carries the lighter components up the column. Anything heavy that rides along cools and falls back down as liquid.


The team with the best recovery got extra credit. More heat pushes more product out the top, but only up to a point. Past it, the column floods, ruining the separation. We had no monitors and no alarms. Every measurement was taken by hand, in between calculations. Every adjustment meant someone turning a valve.


That left two choices. We could stay well back from the limit and settle for an average recovery, or keep turning up the heat and hope.


We found the flood point. The vapor bubbled so violently through the liquid that it foamed to the top of the column almost before we knew what was happening. We pushed for the best recovery and got the worst.


## Margin isn’t free


Real columns are steel, not glass. Engineers track what’s happening inside with instruments that continuously measure pressure, temperature, and flow. They control a unit far more precisely than students turning valves after a hand calculation. Even so, they run a safe distance below the flood point. That distance is the safety margin.


But that margin has a price. It’s capacity you paid for and can’t use. Years later, at a refinery, one column was often the bottleneck for the whole plant, so how close we could safely run it set how much crude oil we could process. Every bit of margin on that column was throughput the plant never got.


Software teams pay this margin too. Change freezes, line-by-line review of every pull request, and the unwritten rule against deploying on Fridays are each a reasonable response to a system you can’t see well or change safely. Each one costs throughput.


Review is the biggest of them, and it looks a lot like our lab. Every check is done by hand, in between other work. For years, it barely registered, because writing code was the slow step and review sat off the bottleneck. AI moved the bottleneck. On many teams, review is now the slowest step, and the margin a team keeps there limits everything it ships.


## The case for reading every line


The argument goes like this. Tests and monitors tell you the code works, but they don’t tell you it’s good code. A change can pass every check and still add a third way of doing something the codebase already does twice, or quietly tie together two parts of the system that were built to stay separate.


Does it matter? It might. But reading every line isn’t the only way to see that cost. It shows up in the process too, just on a different timescale. A process can go wrong in two ways, and the right signal shows both.


## Slop and fouling


Operators watch one signal, called pressure drop, to stay off the flood point. It climbs as vapor and liquid fight for the same space. A sudden spike in pressure drop means the column is flooding now, and anything made in the meantime misses spec. Refineries call that slop, and it has to be reprocessed.


A slow climb over months means something else. Deposits build up inside the column as it runs, and refiners call this fouling. The pressure drop creeps higher, the column inches closer to flooding, and you have to cut throughput to keep your margin. No single day’s product is bad. The unit just runs a little worse each week.


Software’s pressure drop is rework: the share of changes that fail a check or have to be fixed, reverted, or redone later. Like pressure drop, rework can spike or slowly climb, and each needs a different tool.


**A spike signals slop.** In software, slop is a change that fails a test or sets off a monitor and has to be reworked. Slop happens one change at a time, so it can be caught one change at a time. Plants learned long ago that serious incidents cluster around change, which is why every change to a running unit goes through a formal Management of Change process. Software’s version is staged pipelines with testing gates, canaries, feature flags, and automated rollback. And unlike the people stuck reviewing, they don’t get tired by the fortieth PR of the day.


**A slow climb signals fouling.** In software, fouling is tech debt. Every change passed its gate, and the system still got worse. No gate catches it, because no single change caused it. A careful reviewer might catch the third copy, but they can’t tell you whether it’s costing anything. Only a process signal watched over months shows that. Rework creeps up. Agents need more retries and tokens for the same size change. Changes take a little longer to land, and the test suite runs slower every month.


Refineries don’t treat fouling as a failure. They plan a cleaning when the lost throughput starts costing more than the downtime, and tech debt deserves the same call. So does the third copy matter? Watch the trend. It will tell you when.


## Run closer


In the lab, we could see right into the column and still flooded it. Our readings were slow, and our only control was a hand on a valve. With nothing better, a big margin was the only safe move, and we skipped it.


Software teams aren’t stuck like we were. Good observability shows you where the limit is, and good change management lets you back off the moment you get too close. Build both, and you don’t have to choose between margin and hope.
